reminder: A modular function is a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) on the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane) that is invariant under $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and meromorphic at the [cusps](c:cusp).
definition: A modular function for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ is a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) $f$ on the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane) with $f\big(\tfrac{az+b}{cz+d}\big)=f(z)$ for all integers $a,b,c,d$ with $ad-bc=1$. It is also meromorphic at the [cusp](c:cusp) $\infty$: its expansion $f=\sum_{n\ge -N}a_nq^n$ in $q=e^{2\pi i z}$ has only finitely many negative powers. Equivalently, it is a quotient of two [modular forms](c:modular-form) of the same weight.
examples: The [j-invariant](c:j-invariant) $j(z)=q^{-1}+744+196884q+\cdots$ is a modular function with a simple pole at $\infty$ and no other pole.
Every rational function of $j$ is a modular function, and every modular function for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ has this form.
Non-example: the discriminant form $\Delta$ is a modular form of weight $12$, so $\Delta(\gamma z)=(cz+d)^{12}\Delta(z)$; it is not invariant, so it is not a modular function.

steps: Take a modular function $f$, which is meromorphic on the upper half plane $\mathbb{H}$ by definition.
So $f$ is a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) on the open set $\mathbb{H}$.
The modular case adds invariance under every matrix of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
It also adds that the pole order at the cusp $\infty$ is finite.
links.why: It shows that a modular function is a meromorphic function with two extra conditions: a symmetry and controlled growth at the cusp.

steps: Write the [j-invariant](c:j-invariant) as $j=E_4^3/\Delta$, a quotient of two modular forms of weight $12$.
A quotient of two modular forms of the same weight is invariant under $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
The only pole of $j$ is a simple pole at the cusp $\infty$, so $j$ is meromorphic there.
So $j$ is a modular function, and every other modular function is a rational function of $j$.
links.why: It shows that the j-invariant is the basic modular function, from which all others come.

reminder: A moduli space of flat connections parametrizes the flat $G$-connections on a space $X$ up to gauge equivalence.
definition: Let $X$ be a space and $G$ a [group](c:group). A [flat connection](c:flat-connection) on $X$, also called a $G$-[local system](c:local-system), is a map $\Pi(X)\to\mathbf{B}G$ from the fundamental groupoid of $X$. The moduli space of flat connections is the [moduli space](c:moduli-space) or [moduli stack](c:moduli-stack) whose points are the flat connections and whose identifications are their isomorphisms. For connected $X$ and a base point, its set of isomorphism classes is $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X),G)/G$, with $G$ acting by conjugation.
examples: For $X=S^1$ and $G=U(1)$, a flat connection is fixed by its holonomy, so the moduli space is the circle $U(1)$.
For $X=S^1$ and any group $G$, the points are the elements of $G$ up to conjugation.
For a simply connected $X$, every flat connection is trivial, so the moduli space has one point; as a stack it is $\mathbf{B}G$.
Non-example: the moduli space of all connections on a bundle is much bigger; a connection with nonzero curvature is not a point of the moduli space of flat connections.

steps: Take a flat connection on a principal bundle; it is in particular a connection.
Isomorphic flat connections are isomorphic as connections, so the flat points form a subspace of the [moduli space of connections](c:moduli-space-of-connections).
This subspace is cut out by one condition: the curvature of the connection is zero.
links.why: It shows that the flat case is the subspace of curvature-zero points inside the space of all connections.

reminder: A monoidal Quillen adjunction is a [Quillen adjunction](c:quillen-adjunction) between [monoidal model categories](c:monoidal-model-category) whose left adjoint is strong monoidal and respects the unit.
definition: A monoidal Quillen adjunction is a [Quillen adjunction](c:quillen-adjunction) $F\dashv U$ between [monoidal model categories](c:monoidal-model-category) in which $F$ is a strong [monoidal functor](c:monoidal-functor), so that $U$ is canonically [lax monoidal](c:lax-monoidal-functor). It also satisfies a unit condition: for a cofibrant replacement $QI\to I$ of the unit, the map $F(QI)\to F(I)\cong I'$ is a weak equivalence.
examples: The adjunction $|{-}|\dashv\mathrm{Sing}$ between simplicial sets and compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces, with cartesian products, is a monoidal Quillen adjunction, because geometric realization preserves finite products.
The free simplicial abelian group functor $\mathbb{Z}[-]$ from simplicial sets to simplicial abelian groups is strong monoidal and left Quillen, so it gives a monoidal Quillen adjunction.

Non-example: in the Dold-Kan adjunction, a Quillen equivalence between simplicial abelian groups and chain complexes, the normalized chains functor is only lax monoidal, so it is not a monoidal Quillen adjunction in the strict sense.

steps: Start with a monoidal Quillen adjunction $F\dashv U$.
Its left adjoint $F$ preserves cofibrations and trivial cofibrations, so it is a [Quillen adjunction](c:quillen-adjunction).
The monoidal case adds that $F$ is strong monoidal and respects the unit up to weak equivalence.
links.why: It shows that all results about Quillen adjunctions apply, and that the monoidal case adds compatibility with the tensor product.

reminder: A monomial representation is a representation in which every group element acts by a [monomial matrix](c:monomial-matrix) in one fixed basis.
definition: A [representation](c:group-representation) $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is monomial when $V$ has a basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$ that $G$ permutes up to nonzero scalars, so that each $\rho(g)$ is a [monomial matrix](c:monomial-matrix). Equivalently, $V$ is a direct sum of representations [induced](c:induced-representation) from one-dimensional representations of subgroups of finite index.
examples: Every one-dimensional representation is monomial, since a $1\times1$ matrix is a nonzero scalar.
Every [permutation representation](c:permutation-representation) is monomial, since its matrices are permutation matrices.
The two-dimensional irreducible representation of $S_3$ is monomial: it is induced from a nontrivial character of $A_3$.

Non-example: the two-dimensional irreducible complex representations of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_3)$ are not monomial, because an irreducible monomial representation of dimension $2$ is induced from a subgroup of index $2$, and this group has none.

steps: Take a monomial representation $\rho$ with a basis permuted up to scalars.
Each $\rho(g)$ is an invertible matrix, so $\rho$ is a [representation](c:group-representation).
The monomial case adds that every $\rho(g)$ has exactly one nonzero entry in each row and column.
links.why: It shows that general representation theory applies, and that monomiality is a condition on the shape of the matrices.

steps: Start with a [permutation representation](c:permutation-representation), where $G$ permutes a basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$.
Each $\rho(g)$ sends $e_i$ to a basis vector $e_{\sigma(i)}$ with scalar $1$.
So $\rho(g)$ is a monomial matrix whose nonzero entries all equal $1$.
Hence the representation is monomial; the monomial case allows other nonzero scalars.
links.why: It shows that monomial representations extend permutation representations by allowing scalar factors.

reminder: A Morse-Smale system is a [flow](c:flow) whose nonwandering set is finitely many hyperbolic equilibria and periodic orbits, with transversal stable and unstable manifolds.
definition: A smooth [flow](c:flow) on a compact [manifold](c:compact-manifold) is Morse-Smale when its nonwandering set consists of finitely many [hyperbolic equilibria](c:hyperbolic-equilibrium) and [periodic orbits](c:periodic-orbit). A point is nonwandering when each neighborhood of it returns to itself at arbitrarily large times. In addition, the stable manifold of each of these pieces meets the unstable manifold of every other piece [transversally](c:transversality).
examples: On the circle, the flow of $\dot\theta=\sin\theta$ has one source and one sink, so it is Morse-Smale.
The gradient flow of the height function on a round sphere has one source and one sink, so it is Morse-Smale.
On the sphere, the flow $\dot r=r(1-r^2)$, $\dot\theta=1$ has two sources, at $0$ and $\infty$, and one attracting limit cycle $r=1$, so it is Morse-Smale.
Non-example: the linear flow on the torus with irrational slope has every point nonwandering, so its nonwandering set is not a finite union of equilibria and periodic orbits.

steps: Take a Morse-Smale system; it is a smooth [flow](c:flow) on a compact manifold.
The Morse-Smale case adds that the nonwandering set has finitely many hyperbolic pieces.
It also adds that the stable and unstable manifolds of these pieces meet transversally.
links.why: It shows that Morse-Smale systems are the flows with the simplest recurrence and the most generic crossings.

reminder: Natural deduction is a proof system in which a proof starts from assumptions and uses introduction and elimination rules for each connective.
definition: A natural deduction system is a [deductive system](c:deductive-system) that proves judgments $\Gamma\vdash A$ by rules of two kinds. For each logical connective, an introduction rule says how to prove a statement with that connective, and an elimination rule says how to use such a statement. A derivation is a tree of rule steps that may use [hypotheses](c:hypothesis) and later discharge them.
examples: Implication introduction: from a derivation of $B$ that uses the hypothesis $A$, conclude $A\to B$ and discharge $A$.
Conjunction elimination: from $A\wedge B$ conclude $A$, and from $A\wedge B$ conclude $B$.
A derivation of $A\to(B\to A)$: assume $A$, assume $B$, keep $A$, then discharge $B$ and then $A$.

Non-example: a Hilbert-style system with axiom schemes and the single rule modus ponens has no pairs of introduction and elimination rules and no discharge of hypotheses, so it is not natural deduction.

steps: Take a natural deduction system with its language of formulas and its rules.
Its derivations are built from hypotheses by rules, so it is a [deductive system](c:deductive-system).
The natural deduction case adds an introduction rule and an elimination rule for each connective, and the discharge of hypotheses.
links.why: It shows what is special in natural deduction: reasoning from assumptions, with rules in introduction and elimination pairs.

reminder: A nilmanifold is a coset space $G/\Gamma$ of a [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-group) [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ by a closed subgroup $\Gamma$.
definition: A nilmanifold is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) that is diffeomorphic to a [homogeneous space](c:homogeneous-space) $G/\Gamma$, where $G$ is a [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-group) [Lie group](c:lie-group) and $\Gamma\subseteq G$ is a closed subgroup; equivalently, $G$ acts smoothly and transitively on it. In the compact case, one takes $G$ simply connected and $\Gamma$ a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup), that is, a discrete subgroup with compact quotient.
examples: The torus $\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$ is a compact nilmanifold: here $G=\mathbb{R}^n$ is abelian, so it is nilpotent.
The quotient $H_3(\mathbb{R})/H_3(\mathbb{Z})$ of the [Heisenberg group](c:heisenberg-group) by its integer matrices is a compact $3$-dimensional nilmanifold.
The Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n=\mathbb{R}^n/\{0\}$ is a noncompact nilmanifold.
Non-example: the sphere $S^2$ is not a nilmanifold, because every nilmanifold is aspherical while $\pi_2(S^2)\neq0$.

steps: Take a nilmanifold $G/\Gamma$ with $G$ nilpotent.
The group $G$ acts smoothly and transitively on $G/\Gamma$ by left translation.
So $G/\Gamma$ is a [homogeneous space](c:homogeneous-space) of $G$.
The nilmanifold case adds that the acting group $G$ is nilpotent.
links.why: It shows that nilmanifolds are the homogeneous spaces of nilpotent Lie groups.

steps: Take $G=\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^n$.
The group $\mathbb{R}^n$ is abelian, so it is nilpotent, and $\mathbb{Z}^n$ is a lattice.
The quotient $\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$ is the $n$-torus, so every torus is a nilmanifold.
links.why: It shows that tori are the abelian case, and that nilmanifolds allow noncommutative nilpotent groups.

reminder: A [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring) [local ring](c:local-ring) is a ring with exactly one [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) in which every ideal is finitely generated.
definition: A Noetherian local ring is a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $(R,\mathfrak m)$ that is both a [local ring](c:local-ring), with a unique [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak m$, and a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring), so every [ideal](c:ideal) is finitely generated. In particular $\mathfrak m$ is finitely generated, and $R/\mathfrak m$ is a field.
examples: Every field is a Noetherian local ring, with maximal ideal $0$.
The power series ring $k[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$ and the localization $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]_{(x_1,\dots,x_n)}$ are Noetherian local rings.
The ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$ of $p$-adic integers and the localization $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ are Noetherian local rings.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is Noetherian but not local, since $(2)$ and $(3)$ are maximal ideals; the localization of $k[x_1,x_2,\dots]$ at $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ is local but not Noetherian.

steps: Take a Noetherian local ring $R$.
It has a unique maximal ideal, so it is a [local ring](c:local-ring).
The Noetherian case adds that every ideal, including the maximal ideal, is finitely generated.
links.why: It shows that every result about local rings applies, and that finite generation is the added condition.

steps: Take a Noetherian local ring $R$.
Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated, so $R$ is a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring).
The local case adds that $R$ has exactly one maximal ideal.
links.why: It shows that every result about Noetherian rings applies, and that having one maximal ideal is the added condition.

reminder: A normal integral basis of a [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) of number fields is an integral basis formed by the conjugates of one integer.
definition: Let $L/K$ be a [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) of [number fields](c:number-field) with [Galois group](c:galois-group) $G$. A normal integral basis is a basis $\{\sigma(\alpha):\sigma\in G\}$ of the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathcal{O}_L$ over $\mathcal{O}_K$, for one element $\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_L$. Equivalently, $\mathcal{O}_L$ is a free module of rank one over the [group ring](c:group-ring) $\mathcal{O}_K[G]$.
examples: For $L=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $p$ prime, the conjugates $\zeta_p,\zeta_p^2,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-1}$ of $\alpha=\zeta_p$ form a normal integral basis of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$.
For $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt5)/\mathbb{Q}$, the conjugates of $\alpha=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ form a normal integral basis, because their discriminant $5$ equals the field discriminant.

Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}(i)/\mathbb{Q}$ has no normal integral basis, because for $\alpha=a+bi$ the pair $\alpha,\bar\alpha$ spans a sublattice of $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ of index $2|ab|$, which is never $1$.

reminder: A subset of a [topological space](c:topological-space) is nowhere dense when the [interior](c:interior) of its [closure](c:closure) is empty.
definition: A subset $A$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is nowhere dense when $\operatorname{Int}(\operatorname{Cl}(A))=\emptyset$. Equivalently, the [closure](c:closure) of $A$ contains no nonempty open set, so $A$ is not [dense](c:dense-set) in any nonempty open subset of $X$.
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ are nowhere dense in $\mathbb{R}$, since $\mathbb{Z}$ is closed and has empty interior.
The Cantor set is nowhere dense in $[0,1]$.
A line in the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ is nowhere dense.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ is not nowhere dense in $\mathbb{R}$, because its closure is $\mathbb{R}$, which has nonempty interior.

steps: Take a nowhere dense set $A$.
The family $\{A\}$ is a countable family of nowhere dense sets with union $A$.
So $A$ is a countable union of nowhere dense sets, which is a [meager set](c:meager-set).
links.why: It shows that nowhere dense sets are the building blocks of meager sets.

reminder: A null congruence is a smooth family of null curves that fills a region of a Lorentzian manifold with exactly one curve through each point.
definition: Let $U$ be a region of a [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) with metric $g$. A null congruence on $U$ is a smooth family of curves such that exactly one curve passes through each point of $U$ and the tangent vector $k$ of each curve is null, $g(k,k)=0$. It is geodesic when every curve is a null [geodesic](c:geodesic), which is the case that theorems such as the Goldberg-Sachs theorem use.
examples: In Minkowski space, the lines in the direction $\partial_t+\partial_x$ form a null congruence.
In Minkowski space, the outgoing radial light rays $t-r=u$ fill the region $r>0$ and form a geodesic null congruence.
The two principal null congruences of the Kerr solution are geodesic null congruences.

Non-example: the worldlines of observers at rest in Minkowski space form a congruence of timelike curves, not a null congruence, because their tangent $\partial_t$ has $g(\partial_t,\partial_t)\neq0$.

reminder: In an o-minimal structure, every [definable set](c:definable-set) in one variable is a finite union of points and [intervals](c:interval).
definition: Let $(R,<)$ be a [dense linear order](c:dense-linear-order) without endpoints. An o-minimal structure on $R$ is a [structure](c:structure-model-theory) $\mathcal{S}$ on $R$ in which the order is definable and every [definable set](c:definable-set) $A\subseteq R$ is a finite union of points and open intervals with endpoints in $R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$. Here definable means definable with parameters from $R$.
examples: The ordered field $(\mathbb{R},<,+,\cdot)$ is o-minimal: its definable subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are the finite unions of points and intervals (Tarski-Seidenberg).
The expansion $(\mathbb{R},<,+,\cdot,\exp)$ of the real field by the exponential function is o-minimal (Wilkie).
The dense order $(\mathbb{Q},<)$ is o-minimal.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{R},<,+,\cdot,\sin)$ is not o-minimal, because the zero set of $\sin$ is the infinite discrete set $\pi\mathbb{Z}$, which is not a finite union of points and intervals.

steps: Take an o-minimal structure $\mathcal{S}$ on $R$.
It is a [structure](c:structure-model-theory) in the sense of model theory, with an order relation.
The o-minimal case adds a finiteness condition on the definable subsets of the line.
links.why: It shows that o-minimality is a tameness condition added to an ordinary structure.

reminder: The one-point compactification of a space $X$ adds one point $\infty$, whose neighborhoods are the complements of closed [compact](c:compact-space) subsets of $X$.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space). Its one-point compactification is $X^*=X\cup\{\infty\}$ with this topology: a set is open when it is open in $X$, or when it is $X^*\setminus K$ for a closed [compact](c:compact-space) set $K\subseteq X$. The space $X^*$ is always [compact](c:compact-space), and it is a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) exactly when $X$ is a [locally compact](c:locally-compact-space) Hausdorff space.
examples: The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has the sphere $S^n$ as its one-point compactification, by stereographic projection.
The open interval $(0,1)$ has the circle as its one-point compactification: the two ends merge into the point $\infty$.
The discrete space $\mathbb{N}$ has as one-point compactification the convergent sequence $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ is not locally compact, and $\mathbb{Q}^*$ is compact but not Hausdorff, because every neighborhood of $\infty$ meets every nonempty open set of $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps: Take a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$ that is not compact.
Then $X^*$ is a compact Hausdorff space that contains $X$ as an open dense subspace.
So $X^*$ is a [compactification](c:compactification) of $X$, the one that adds a single point.
links.why: It shows that the one-point compactification is the smallest compactification of a locally compact Hausdorff space.

steps: Start with a linear representation $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ of a topological group $G$.
Form the one-point compactification $V^*=V\cup\{\infty\}$, which is the sphere $S^n$.
Each $g\in G$ acts on $V$ by a homeomorphism, and it extends to $V^*$ by $g\cdot\infty=\infty$.
The result is the [representation sphere](c:representation-sphere), a $G$-space whose underlying space is $S^n$.
links.why: It shows that a representation sphere is a one-point compactification that remembers the group action.

reminder: The orbit type of a point is the isomorphism class of its [orbit](c:orbit) as a $G$-space, that is, the conjugacy class of its stabilizer.
definition: Let a [group](c:group) $G$ act on a space $X$. The orbit type of $x\in X$ is the isomorphism class of the $G$-space $G\cdot x\cong G/G_x$, where $G_x$ is the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) of $x$. Two points have the same orbit type exactly when their stabilizers lie in the same [conjugacy class](c:conjugacy-class) of subgroups of $G$.
examples: Let $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ rotate the plane. The origin has orbit type $G/G$, a point, and every other point has orbit type $G/e$, a free orbit that is a circle.
Let $\mathbb{Z}/2$ act on the circle by a reflection. The two fixed points have orbit type $G/G$, and all other points have orbit type $G/e$.
Let $S_3$ permute the coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Points with three equal coordinates, with exactly two equal coordinates and with three distinct coordinates have three different orbit types.
Non-example: the stabilizer $G_x$ itself is not the orbit type, because $G_{gx}=gG_xg^{-1}$ can differ from $G_x$ although $x$ and $gx$ lie in one orbit.

reminder: An orthomodular space is a space with a [Hermitian form](c:hermitian-form) in which every subspace $U$ with $U=U^{\perp\perp}$ satisfies $U\oplus U^\perp=V$.
definition: Let $V$ be a vector space over a [division ring](c:division-ring) $K$ with an [involution](c:involution), with an anisotropic [Hermitian form](c:hermitian-form), so that $\langle x,x\rangle=0$ only for $x=0$. Call a subspace $U$ closed when $U=U^{\perp\perp}$, where $U^\perp$ is its orthogonal complement. Then $V$ is orthomodular when $U\oplus U^\perp=V$ for every closed subspace $U$.
examples: Every [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) over $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or the quaternions is orthomodular: for a closed subspace $U$, the projection theorem gives $H=U\oplus U^\perp$.
Every finite-dimensional space with a positive definite form, such as $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product, is orthomodular.
Non-example: the Minkowski plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\langle x,y\rangle=x_1y_1-x_2y_2$ is not orthomodular: for the line $U$ spanned by $(1,1)$ one has $U^\perp=U$, so $U\oplus U^\perp\neq V$.

steps: Take a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ over $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or the quaternions, with its inner product.
The inner product is an anisotropic Hermitian form over a division ring with involution.
For a closed subspace $U$, the projection theorem gives $H=U\oplus U^\perp$.
So $H$ is an orthomodular space.
links.why: It shows that orthomodular spaces include all Hilbert spaces, and Solèr's theorem says that an infinite orthonormal sequence gives back exactly these.

reminder: A p-adic L-function is a p-adic analytic function that interpolates the values of an [L-function](c:l-function) at negative integers.
definition: Fix an odd prime $p$ and an even [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character) $\chi$. The Kubota-Leopoldt $p$-adic $L$-function $L_p(s,\chi)$ is the function of $s\in\mathbb{Z}_p$, with values in $\mathbb{C}_p$, that is analytic (with a simple pole at $s=1$ if $\chi$ is trivial) and satisfies $L_p(1-n,\chi)=(1-\chi\omega^{-n}(p)p^{n-1})\,L(1-n,\chi\omega^{-n})$ for all $n\ge1$, where $\omega$ is the Teichmüller character. It is a function of a [p-adic integer](c:p-adic-integer) variable, not of a complex variable.
examples: The $p$-adic zeta function $\zeta_p(s)=L_p(s,1)$ satisfies $\zeta_p(1-n)=-(1-p^{n-1})B_n/n$ when $p-1$ divides $n$, which is a Bernoulli number with its Euler factor at $p$ removed.
For an even character $\chi\neq1$, the function $L_p(s,\chi)$ has no pole and is analytic on all of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
Non-example: the classical function $L(s,\chi)$ is not a $p$-adic $L$-function, because it takes complex values at complex arguments.

reminder: A p-adic power series is a series $\sum a_nx^n$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}_p$ that is evaluated at $p$-adic points where its terms tend to $0$.
definition: A p-adic power series is a [power series](c:power-series) $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ with coefficients $a_n$ in $\mathbb{Q}_p$ or $\mathbb{C}_p$. It converges at $x$ exactly when $|a_nx^n|_p\to0$, because the [p-adic](c:p-adic-number) absolute value is ultrametric. If $a_n\to0$, it converges at every $x$ with $|x|_p\le1$, in particular on $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
examples: The series $\sum_{n\ge0}p^nx^n$ has $a_n\to0$, so it converges for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}_p$, with value $1/(1-px)$.
The exponential series $\sum x^n/n!$ converges exactly for $|x|_p<p^{-1/(p-1)}$.
The logarithm series $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}x^n/n$ converges exactly for $|x|_p<1$.
Non-example: the series $\sum x^n$ does not define a function on all of $\mathbb{Z}_p$, because its terms do not tend to $0$ at $x=1$.

steps: Take a p-adic power series $\sum a_nx^n$ with $a_n\in\mathbb{Q}_p$.
It is a [power series](c:power-series) over the field $\mathbb{Q}_p$.
The p-adic case adds convergence in the p-adic absolute value, so the series also defines a function on a disc.
links.why: It shows that formal facts about power series hold, and that analytic facts need the p-adic absolute value.

reminder: The p-completion of an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $A$ is the inverse limit of the quotients $A/p^nA$.
definition: For an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $A$ and a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$, the p-completion is $A^\wedge_p=\varprojlim_n A/p^nA$, the [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of the quotients $A/p^nA$ along the reduction maps. For a spectrum $X$, the p-completion $X^\wedge_p=\varprojlim_n X/p^n$ is its localization at mod $p$ homology, and its homotopy groups are the derived $p$-completions of those of $X$.
examples: The p-completion of $\mathbb{Z}$ is the ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$ of $p$-adic integers.
The p-completion of a finite abelian group is its $p$-primary part: $\mathbb{Z}/p^k$ stays as it is, and $\mathbb{Z}/q$ with $q\ne p$ goes to $0$.
For the sphere spectrum $S$, the p-completion $S^\wedge_p$ has $\pi_0=\mathbb{Z}_p$.
Non-example: the localization $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ is not $p$-complete, because its p-completion is the larger ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$.

steps: Take the ideal $I=(p)$ of the ring $\mathbb{Z}$.
The $I$-adic [completion of a module](c:completion-of-a-module) $A$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ is $\varprojlim A/I^nA=\varprojlim A/p^nA$.
An abelian group is a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, so this limit is the p-completion of $A$.
links.why: It shows that the p-completion is the ideal-adic completion for the ideal generated by one prime.

steps: Take the abelian group $\mathbb{Z}$.
Its p-completion is the inverse limit $\varprojlim\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$.
This inverse limit is the ring of [p-adic integers](c:p-adic-integer).
links.why: It shows that the p-adic integers are the p-completion of the integers.

reminder: A permutation group is a set of [permutations](c:permutation) of a set that contains the identity and is closed under composition and inverses.
definition: A permutation group on a set $X$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ of all bijections $X\to X$. So it is a set of [permutations](c:permutation) of $X$ that contains the identity and is closed under composition and inverses. By Cayley's theorem, every [group](c:group) is isomorphic to a permutation group, through its action on itself.
examples: The symmetric group $S_n$ and the alternating group $A_n$ are permutation groups on $\{1,\dots,n\}$.
The rotations of a square, acting on its four vertices, form the cyclic permutation group generated by $(1\,2\,3\,4)$.
The dihedral group of the square acts on its four vertices as a permutation group of order $8$.
Non-example: the set $\{e,(1\,2),(2\,3)\}$ is not a permutation group, because the product $(1\,2)(2\,3)$ is a $3$-cycle outside the set.

steps: Take a permutation group $P\le\mathrm{Sym}(X)$.
Composition of bijections is associative, the identity lies in $P$, and $P$ contains inverses.
So $P$ is a [group](c:group) under composition.
The permutation case adds a faithful action on a set $X$; Cayley's theorem shows that every group has one.
links.why: It shows that permutation groups are groups with a chosen faithful action, and that no group is lost.

steps: Take a set $X$ and its [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$.
It is a subgroup of itself, so it contains the identity and is closed under composition and inverses.
So $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ is a permutation group, the largest one on $X$.
links.why: It shows that the symmetric group is the biggest permutation group, and every other one sits inside it.

reminder: A $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-module is a module over a ring of $p$-adic Laurent series with a Frobenius map $\varphi$ and a commuting action of $\Gamma$.
definition: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the field of Laurent series in $T$ over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ that are bounded and have coefficients tending to $0$ at $-\infty$, with the [Frobenius](c:frobenius) $\varphi(T)=(1+T)^p-1$ and the action of $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}_p^\times$ given by $\gamma(T)=(1+T)^\gamma-1$. A $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-module is a finite-dimensional $\mathcal{E}$-vector space $D$ with a $\varphi$-semilinear map $\varphi:D\to D$ and a commuting, continuous, semilinear [action](c:group-action) of $\Gamma$. It is étale when $D$ has a lattice over the integers of $\mathcal{E}$ that is stable under $\varphi$ and $\Gamma$ and generated by its image under $\varphi$.
examples: The module $D=\mathcal{E}$, with $\varphi$ and $\Gamma$ acting as on $\mathcal{E}$, is a rank-one étale $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-module; it matches the trivial one-dimensional $p$-adic representation of $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/\mathbb{Q}_p)$.

By Fontaine's equivalence, each $p$-adic [Galois representation](c:galois-representation) $V$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/\mathbb{Q}_p)$ gives an étale $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-module $D(V)$ of rank $\dim V$, and every étale module arises this way.
Non-example: a finite-dimensional $\mathcal{E}$-vector space with a semilinear $\varphi$ but no action of $\Gamma$ is only a $\varphi$-module, not a $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-module.

reminder: A function is approximated by [polynomials](c:polynomial) on a set when polynomials come arbitrarily close to it in the supremum distance on that set.
definition: A function $f$ on a set $K$ can be approximated by [polynomials](c:polynomial) on $K$ when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some polynomial $p$ satisfies $\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-p(x)|<\varepsilon$. Equivalently, $f$ is the [uniform limit](c:uniform-convergence) on $K$ of a sequence of polynomials. The classical questions ask which functions $f$ and which sets $K$ allow this.
examples: Every [continuous function](c:continuous-function) on a closed interval $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials (Weierstrass).
The function $|x|$ on $[-1,1]$ is approximated by polynomials, although it is not differentiable at $0$.
On every compact subset of $\mathbb{C}$, the function $e^z$ is approximated by its Taylor polynomials.
Non-example: $f(z)=1/z$ on the unit circle is not approximated by polynomials in $z$: for every polynomial $p$, $\sup_{|z|=1}|1/z-p(z)|\ge1$, because $\oint(1/z-p(z))\,dz=2\pi i$.

reminder: A [prime number](c:prime-number) is a primitive prime divisor of the $n$th term of a sequence when it divides that term but no earlier term.
definition: Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be an integer [sequence](c:sequence), such as the [Fibonacci numbers](c:fibonacci-numbers) or $2^n-1$. A [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ is a primitive prime divisor of $a_n$ when $p$ [divides](c:divisibility) $a_n$ but does not divide $a_m$ for any $m$ with $1\le m<n$.
examples: In the Fibonacci numbers $1,1,2,3,5,8,13,\dots$, the prime $5$ is a primitive prime divisor of $F_5=5$, because $5$ divides none of $F_1,\dots,F_4$.
For $F_{10}=55=5\cdot11$, the prime $11$ is primitive, but $5$ is not, because $5$ already divides $F_5$.
Carmichael's theorem says that $F_n$ has a primitive prime divisor for every $n$ except $1$, $2$, $6$ and $12$.
Non-example: $2^6-1=63=3^2\cdot7$ has no primitive prime divisor, because $3$ divides $2^2-1$ and $7$ divides $2^3-1$.

reminder: A product of two objects has two projections such that every pair of maps into them factors uniquely through it.
definition: In a [category](c:category), a product of objects $X$ and $Y$ is an object $X\times Y$ with morphisms $\pi_1:X\times Y\to X$ and $\pi_2:X\times Y\to Y$. For every object $T$ and all morphisms $f:T\to X$ and $g:T\to Y$, there is exactly one morphism $h:T\to X\times Y$ with $\pi_1h=f$ and $\pi_2h=g$. This is a [universal property](c:universal-property), so the product is unique up to unique isomorphism, and the same definition works for any family of objects.
examples: In the category of sets, the product is the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) with the two coordinate projections.
In the category of topological spaces, the product is the product space; in the category of groups, it is the direct product.
In a poset viewed as a category, the product of $x$ and $y$ is their [meet](c:meet), the greatest lower bound, when it exists.
Non-example: in the category of sets, the disjoint union $X\sqcup Y$ with its two inclusions is not a product; it is the coproduct, and its arrows go in the wrong direction.

steps: Take the category of sets and two sets $X$ and $Y$.
The set $X\times Y$ with its two coordinate maps is a candidate for the product.
Given $f:T\to X$ and $g:T\to Y$, the map $t\mapsto(f(t),g(t))$ is the only map that is compatible with both projections.
So the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) is the categorical product in the category of sets.
links.why: It shows that the categorical product is the universal property that the Cartesian product of sets satisfies, now stated in any category.

steps: Take the discrete diagram with two objects $X$ and $Y$ and no arrows between them.
A cone over this diagram is an object $T$ with maps $f:T\to X$ and $g:T\to Y$.
A [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of the diagram is a cone through which every cone factors uniquely.
That is exactly the product $X\times Y$ with its projections.
links.why: It shows that products are the limits of diagrams with no arrows, so every theorem about limits applies to them.

reminder: The projective linear group $\mathrm{PGL}_n(K)$ is the quotient of the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ by its nonzero scalar matrices.
definition: For a [field](c:field) $K$ and $n\ge1$, the projective linear group is $\mathrm{PGL}_n(K)=\mathrm{GL}_n(K)/K^\times I$, where $K^\times I$ is the [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of nonzero scalar matrices. It is the group of transformations of the [projective space](c:projective-space) $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(K)$ that come from invertible linear maps of $K^n$.
examples: The group $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ acts on the projective line by the Möbius maps $x\mapsto(ax+b)/(cx+d)$ with $ad-bc\neq0$.
The groups $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{F}_3)$ are isomorphic to $S_3$ and $S_4$.
Over $\mathbb{C}$, every scalar has an $n$th root, so $\mathrm{PGL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ equals the projective special linear group $\mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$.
Non-example: $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ itself is not a projective linear group, because the matrix $2I$ acts as the identity on the projective line but is not the identity matrix.

steps: Take $G=\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ and $N=K^\times I$, the group of nonzero scalar matrices.
Scalar matrices commute with every matrix, so $N$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$.
The [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $G/N$ is the projective linear group.
links.why: It shows that the projective linear group is one explicit quotient, so the homomorphism theorems apply to it.

reminder: A proper space is a [metric space](c:metric-space) in which every closed [ball](c:ball) is [compact](c:compact-space).
definition: A [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$, or more generally a pseudometric space, is proper when every closed ball $\{y:d(x,y)\le r\}$ is [compact](c:compact-space). Equivalently, every closed bounded subset of $X$ is compact.
examples: The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric is proper, by the Heine-Borel theorem.
Every compact metric space is proper.
Every complete Riemannian manifold, such as the hyperbolic plane, is proper, with its distance function (Hopf-Rinow).

Non-example: $(0,1)$ with the usual metric is not proper, since the closed ball of radius $1$ about $1/2$ is $(0,1)$, which is not compact; an infinite-dimensional [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) is not proper either.

steps: Take a proper space $X$ and a point $x$.
The closed ball of radius $1$ about $x$ is compact and contains the open ball of radius $1$, a neighborhood of $x$.
So $x$ has a compact neighborhood.
Hence $X$ is a [locally compact space](c:locally-compact-space).
links.why: It shows that properness is a uniform version of local compactness, with the same size of compact neighborhood at every point.

steps: Take a Cauchy sequence in a proper metric space $X$.
It is bounded, so it lies in one closed ball, which is compact.
So a subsequence converges, and a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.
Hence $X$ is a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space).
links.why: It shows that every proper metric space is complete, so limits of Cauchy sequences exist.

reminder: A quasigroup is a set with a binary operation in which each equation $ax=b$ and $ya=b$ has exactly one solution.
definition: A quasigroup is a [magma](c:magma) $(Q,\cdot)$ in which left and right multiplication are [bijections](c:bijection): for all $a,b\in Q$ there is exactly one $x$ with $a\cdot x=b$ and exactly one $y$ with $y\cdot a=b$. It need not be [associative](c:associativity) and need not have an [identity element](c:identity-element). Its multiplication table is a [Latin square](c:latin-square).
examples: Every [group](c:group) is a quasigroup, with the solutions $x=a^{-1}b$ and $y=ba^{-1}$.
The integers with subtraction $a\cdot b=a-b$ form a quasigroup, with solutions $x=a-b$ and $y=a+b$; the operation is not associative.
The multiplication table of a finite quasigroup is a Latin square, and every Latin square is the table of a finite quasigroup.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{N},+)$ is not a quasigroup, because $3+x=2$ has no solution in $\mathbb{N}$.

steps: Take a quasigroup $(Q,\cdot)$.
It has a binary operation $Q\times Q\to Q$, so it is a [magma](c:magma).
The quasigroup case adds that every left and right multiplication is a bijection.
links.why: It shows that a quasigroup is a magma with unique division on both sides.

steps: Start with a quasigroup $Q$ and add the condition that its operation is associative.
Pick $a\in Q$ and solve $ae=a$; then $be=b$ for all $b$, so $e$ is an identity element.
Every element has an inverse, because the equation $ax=e$ has a solution.
So $Q$ is a [group](c:group).
links.why: It shows that a group is a quasigroup with associativity, and that associativity alone gives the identity and the inverses.

reminder: The $i$th ramification group is the set of Galois automorphisms that move every integer of $L$ by an element of valuation at least $i+1$.
definition: Let $L/K$ be a finite [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) of [local fields](c:local-field) with [Galois group](c:galois-group) $G$. Let $v_L$ be the normalized [valuation](c:discrete-valuation) of $L$, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_L$. For an integer $i\ge-1$ the ramification group in the lower numbering is $G_i=\{\sigma\in G: v_L(\sigma(x)-x)\ge i+1\text{ for all }x\in\mathcal{O}_L\}$; these groups are normal in $G$ and form a decreasing chain $G=G_{-1}\supseteq G_0\supseteq G_1\supseteq\cdots$ with $G_i=1$ for large $i$.
examples: For an unramified extension, $G_0=1$, so only $G_{-1}=G$ is nontrivial.
For $\mathbb{Q}_p(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q}_p$, the group $G\cong(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$ has $G_0=G$ and $G_1=1$, because the extension is tamely ramified.
For $\mathbb{Q}_2(i)/\mathbb{Q}_2$ with $G$ of order $2$, one has $G_0=G_1=G$ and $G_2=1$.
Non-example: a non-normal subgroup of $G$, such as a subgroup of order $2$ in $S_3$, is never a ramification group, because every $G_i$ is normal in $G$.

reminder: The rank of a [group](c:group) is the smallest number of elements that generate it.
definition: The rank of a [group](c:group) $G$ is the smallest [cardinal number](c:cardinal-number) $r$ such that $G$ has a generating set with $r$ elements, written $\operatorname{rank}(G)$. For a [finitely generated group](c:finitely-generated-group), this is a natural number.
examples: The group $\mathbb{Z}^n$ has rank $n$, and the trivial group has rank $0$.
The [free group](c:free-group) $F_n$ on $n$ letters has rank $n$.
The symmetric group $S_n$ with $n\ge3$ has rank $2$, generated by a transposition and an $n$-cycle.
Non-example: the generating set $\{2,3\}$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ has two elements, but $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbb{Z})=1$, because the rank counts a smallest generating set and not a given one.

reminder: A rational surface is an [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) that is birational to the projective plane.
definition: An [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) $X$ over a field $k$ is rational when it is birational to the [projective plane](c:projective-space) $\mathbb{P}^2_k$. That is, there is a [birational map](c:birational-map) $X\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^2$, an isomorphism between dense open subsets of $X$ and $\mathbb{P}^2$. Over an algebraically closed field, this means that the function field of $X$ is $k(s,t)$, a purely transcendental extension of $k$ of degree $2$.
examples: The projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2$ and the product $\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1$ are rational surfaces.
The blow-up of $\mathbb{P}^2$ at a point, and every smooth quadric surface in $\mathbb{P}^3$, are rational surfaces.
Every smooth cubic surface in $\mathbb{P}^3$ over $\mathbb{C}$ is rational; it is a [del Pezzo surface](c:del-pezzo-surface).
Non-example: a smooth quartic surface in $\mathbb{P}^3$ over $\mathbb{C}$, a K3 surface, is not rational, because its geometric genus is $1$ while rational surfaces have geometric genus $0$.

steps: Take a rational surface $X$.
It is an [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) by definition.
The rational case adds a birational map from $X$ to the projective plane.
links.why: It shows that rationality is a birational condition on a surface, not an extra structure.

steps: Take a [del Pezzo surface](c:del-pezzo-surface) $X$ over an algebraically closed field.
By the classification, $X$ is $\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1$ or the blow-up of $\mathbb{P}^2$ in at most eight points in general position.
Both are birational to $\mathbb{P}^2$.
So every del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field is a rational surface.
links.why: It shows that del Pezzo surfaces form a large family of rational surfaces with ample anticanonical class.

reminder: A rectifiable curve is a [curve](c:curve) whose length, the supremum of the lengths of its inscribed polygons, is finite.
definition: A [continuous](c:continuous-function) curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to X$ in a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ is rectifiable when its length $L(\gamma)=\sup\sum_{i=1}^{k}d(\gamma(t_{i-1}),\gamma(t_i))$ is finite, where the supremum runs over all partitions $a=t_0<\dots<t_k=b$. In $\mathbb{R}^n$, this means that the coordinate functions have [bounded variation](c:bounded-variation).
examples: Every $C^1$ curve, such as the unit circle, is rectifiable, with length $\int_a^b|\gamma'(t)|\,dt$.
Every polygonal path is rectifiable.
Every [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) curve is rectifiable: its length is at most the Lipschitz constant times $b-a$.
Non-example: the Koch curve has infinite length, and so does the graph of $t\mapsto t\sin(1/t)$ on $[0,1]$, so neither is rectifiable.

steps: Take a rectifiable curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to X$; it is a [curve](c:curve) in $X$.
The rectifiable case adds that the supremum of the polygon lengths is finite.
So the length of $\gamma$ is a real number, and it can be used in integrals and in arc-length parametrization.
links.why: It shows that rectifiable curves are the curves that have a length.

reminder: A Reeb component is a [foliation](c:foliation) of the solid torus whose boundary torus is a leaf and whose other leaves are planes.
definition: The Reeb component is the codimension-one [foliation](c:foliation) of the [solid torus](c:solid-torus) $D^2\times S^1$ built as follows. Take the foliation of $D^2\times\mathbb{R}$ that has the boundary cylinder $\partial D^2\times\mathbb{R}$ as one leaf and the graphs $z=c+1/(1-r^2)$, for $c\in\mathbb{R}$, over the open disc as the other [leaves](c:leaf), and divide by the shift $z\mapsto z+1$. The boundary torus is a compact leaf, and every other leaf is a plane that approaches the boundary torus.
examples: Two Reeb components glued along their boundary tori form the Reeb foliation of the $3$-sphere $S^3$, in which the common torus is the only compact leaf.
Novikov proved that every $C^2$ codimension-one foliation of $S^3$ contains a Reeb component.

Non-example: the product foliation of $D^2\times S^1$ by the discs $D^2\times\{\theta\}$ is not a Reeb component, because its leaves meet the boundary torus transversally, so the boundary is not a leaf.
Non-example: the foliation of the solid torus by concentric tori has the boundary torus as a leaf, but its other leaves are tori, not planes.

steps: Take the Reeb component on the solid torus $D^2\times S^1$.
It splits this $3$-manifold into leaves of dimension $2$, so it is a codimension-one [foliation](c:foliation).
The Reeb case adds that the boundary torus is a compact leaf and that every other leaf is a plane.
links.why: It shows that the Reeb component is a foliation with a compact boundary leaf, which gives foliations of $S^3$ a compact leaf.

reminder: The representation sphere of a representation $V$ of a group $G$ is the [one-point compactification](c:one-point-compactification) of $V$, with the induced $G$-action.
definition: Let $G$ be a [topological group](c:topological-group) acting linearly on $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ by a [representation](c:group-representation), usually an orthogonal one. The representation sphere $S^V$ is the [one-point compactification](c:one-point-compactification) $V\cup\{\infty\}\cong S^n$, with $G$ acting on $V$ as before and fixing the point $\infty$. It is a pointed $G$-space, and both $0$ and $\infty$ are fixed points.
examples: For the trivial representation $\mathbb{R}^n$, the representation sphere is the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$ with trivial action.
For $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$ acting on $\mathbb{R}$ by $x\mapsto-x$, the representation sphere is a circle with a reflection that fixes $0$ and $\infty$.
For $G=S^1$ acting on $\mathbb{C}$ by rotation, the representation sphere is the $2$-sphere with the rotation about the axis through $0$ and $\infty$.
Non-example: the unit sphere $S(V)\subset V$ is not $S^V$; it has dimension $n-1$ and in general has no fixed point, while $S^V$ is the unreduced suspension of $S(V)$ and has two.

steps: Take a representation $V$ of $G$, a space on which $G$ acts by homeomorphisms.
Form its [one-point compactification](c:one-point-compactification) $V^*=V\cup\{\infty\}$.
Each $g\in G$ extends to $V^*$ by $g\cdot\infty=\infty$, and the extension is continuous.
So $V^*$ is a $G$-space; it is the representation sphere.
links.why: It shows that a representation sphere is a one-point compactification together with the induced group action.

reminder: A restricted product of spaces $X_s$ relative to open subspaces $K_s$ consists of the families $(x_s)$ with $x_s\in K_s$ for all but finitely many $s$.
definition: Let $(X_s)_{s\in S}$ be a family of [topological spaces](c:topological-space) with open subspaces $K_s\subseteq X_s$. The restricted product $\prod'_s X_s$ is the subset of the [product](c:product) of all families $(x_s)$ with $x_s\in K_s$ for all but [finitely](c:finite-set) many $s$. Its topology has as a basis the products $\prod_s U_s$ with $U_s\subseteq X_s$ open and $U_s=K_s$ for all but finitely many $s$.
examples: The [ring of adeles](c:ring-of-adeles) of $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{R}\times\prod'_p\mathbb{Q}_p$, where the restricted product is taken relative to the subrings $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
The [group of ideles](c:group-of-ideles) is $\mathbb{R}^\times\times\prod'_p\mathbb{Q}_p^\times$, restricted relative to the subgroups $\mathbb{Z}_p^\times$.
For discrete groups $X_s$ and $K_s=\{0\}$, the restricted product is the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $\bigoplus_sX_s$.
Non-example: the full product $\prod_p\mathbb{Q}_p$ is bigger; the family $(1/p)_p$ lies in it but not in the restricted product, because $1/p\notin\mathbb{Z}_p$ for every $p$.

steps: Take abelian groups $X_s$, each discrete, and the subgroups $K_s=\{0\}$.
A family has $x_s\in K_s$ for almost all $s$ exactly when $x_s=0$ for almost all $s$.
So the restricted product is the set of finitely supported families, which is the [direct sum](c:direct-sum).
links.why: It shows that the direct sum is the restricted product for the smallest choice of subgroups.

steps: Take the spaces $X_p=\mathbb{Q}_p$ with the subrings $K_p=\mathbb{Z}_p$, for all primes $p$.
Their restricted product consists of the families that are $p$-adic integers at almost all primes.
With the real factor $\mathbb{R}$ added, this restricted product is the [ring of adeles](c:ring-of-adeles) of $\mathbb{Q}$.
links.why: It shows that the adeles are a restricted product, which explains their topology.

reminder: A rigid motion is a transformation of the plane or space that keeps the distance between every two points.
definition: A rigid motion of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a bijective [isometry](c:isometry) $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, $|f(x)-f(y)|=|x-y|$ for all $x,y$. Each rigid motion has the form $x\mapsto Ax+b$ with $A$ in the [orthogonal group](c:orthogonal-group) and $b$ a vector; some authors also require $\det A=1$.
examples: A translation $x\mapsto x+b$, a rotation about a point and a reflection in a line are rigid motions.
A glide reflection, which is a reflection followed by a translation along the mirror line, is a rigid motion.
Two figures are congruent when a rigid motion carries one onto the other.
Non-example: the dilation $x\mapsto2x$ is not a rigid motion, because it doubles every distance; the shear $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y,y)$ also changes distances.

steps: Take a rigid motion $f$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
By definition $f$ keeps the distance between any two points, so $f$ is an [isometry](c:isometry).
The rigid motion case adds that $f$ is a bijection of the whole space onto itself, and for some authors that $f$ keeps orientation.
links.why: It shows that a rigid motion is an isometry of Euclidean space onto itself.

reminder: The Schnirelmann density of a set $A$ of natural numbers is the infimum over $n\ge1$ of the ratio $A(n)/n$.
definition: For $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ let $A(n)$ be the number of elements $a\in A$ with $a\le n$; this is the [counting function](c:counting-function) of $A$. The Schnirelmann density of $A$ is $d(A)=\inf_{n\ge1}A(n)/n$. It satisfies $0\le d(A)\le1$, and $d(A)=1$ exactly when $A$ contains all [natural numbers](c:natural-number).
examples: One has $d(\mathbb{N})=1$, and $d(A)=0$ for every set $A$ that misses $1$, because $A(1)=0$.
The odd numbers have $d=1/2$: here $A(n)=\lceil n/2\rceil$, and the ratio is smallest, $1/2$, at even $n$.
The squares $1,4,9,\dots$ have $d=0$, because $A(n)=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ and $A(n)/n\to0$.
Non-example: the Schnirelmann density is not the asymptotic density; the even numbers have asymptotic density $1/2$ but Schnirelmann density $0$, because $1$ is not in the set.

reminder: A [line bundle](c:line-bundle) is semi-ample when some positive power of it is generated by its global sections.
definition: A [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$, also called an invertible [sheaf](c:sheaf), on a [scheme](c:scheme) $X$ is semi-ample when $L^{\otimes m}$ is globally generated for some $m>0$. That is, at every point some global section of $L^{\otimes m}$ does not vanish, so finitely many such sections define a morphism from $X$ to a projective space.
examples: Every [ample line bundle](c:ample-sheaf) on a quasi-compact scheme, such as $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(1)$, is semi-ample.
The trivial bundle $\mathcal{O}_X$ is semi-ample, since the section $1$ generates it; on a projective variety of positive dimension it is not ample.
For the blow-up $\pi:\widetilde{\mathbb{P}^2}\to\mathbb{P}^2$ at a point, the bundle $\pi^*\mathcal{O}(1)$ is semi-ample but not ample, because it has degree $0$ on the exceptional curve.
Non-example: $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-1)$ is not semi-ample, because every power $\mathcal{O}(-m)$ with $m>0$ has no nonzero global section.

steps: Start with an [ample line bundle](c:ample-sheaf) $L$ on a quasi-compact scheme $X$.
By ampleness applied to the coherent sheaf $\mathcal{O}_X$, the bundle $L^{\otimes m}$ is globally generated for large $m$.
So $L$ is semi-ample.
The ample case adds that, for $X$ proper over a field and large $m$, the map defined by $L^{\otimes m}$ is an embedding.
links.why: It shows that a semi-ample bundle gives a morphism to projective space, and that ampleness adds that this morphism is an embedding.

reminder: A semidirect product $N\rtimes G$ is the set $N\times G$ with a product twisted by an action of $G$ on $N$ by automorphisms.
definition: Let $N$ and $G$ be [groups](c:group) and let $\varphi:G\to\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ be a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) into the [automorphism group](c:automorphism-group) of $N$. The semidirect product $N\rtimes_\varphi G$ is the set $N\times G$ with the product $(n_1,g_1)(n_2,g_2)=(n_1\,\varphi(g_1)(n_2),\,g_1g_2)$. In it, $N$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup), $G$ is a complement subgroup, and $G$ acts on $N$ by conjugation through $\varphi$.
examples: The dihedral group is $D_n\cong C_n\rtimes C_2$, where the generator of $C_2$ acts on $C_n$ by inversion.
The Euclidean group of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $\mathbb{R}^n\rtimes O(n)$: translations extended by orthogonal maps.
If $\varphi$ is trivial, then $N\rtimes G=N\times G$ is the [direct product](c:direct-product).
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/4$ is not a semidirect product of two nontrivial groups, because its only nontrivial proper subgroup is $\{0,2\}$, so no two such subgroups meet only in $0$.

steps: Start with a [direct product](c:direct-product) $N\times G$ of groups.
Let $G$ act on $N$ trivially, so $\varphi(g)=\mathrm{id}_N$ for all $g$.
Then the twisted product $(n_1\varphi(g_1)(n_2),g_1g_2)$ equals $(n_1n_2,g_1g_2)$, the product of the direct product.
So the direct product is the semidirect product for the trivial action.
links.why: It shows that the semidirect product adds a twist by an action, which the direct product lacks.

steps: Take $N\rtimes_\varphi G$ with the maps $n\mapsto(n,1)$ and $(n,g)\mapsto g$.
The first map is injective, the second is surjective, and the image of the first is the kernel of the second.
So $1\to N\to N\rtimes G\to G\to1$ is a [group extension](c:group-extension).
The semidirect case adds that the extension splits, by the section $g\mapsto(1,g)$.
links.why: It shows that semidirect products are exactly the split extensions.

reminder: The shear map of an action of a group $G$ on $X$ is the map $G\times X\to X\times X$ given by $(g,x)\mapsto(x,gx)$.
definition: Let a [group](c:group) $G$ act on a set or space $X$ by an [action](c:group-action) $\rho:G\times X\to X$. The shear map is $G\times X\to X\times X$, $(g,x)\mapsto(x,\rho(g,x))$, a map out of the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product). The action is free exactly when the shear map is injective, transitive exactly when it is surjective, and a [pseudo-torsor](c:pseudo-torsor) exactly when it is bijective, or an isomorphism in the ambient category.
examples: For $G$ acting on itself by left multiplication, the shear map $(g,h)\mapsto(h,gh)$ is a bijection, with inverse $(h,k)\mapsto(h^{-1}k,h)$.
For the rotation action of $S^1$ on itself, the shear map is a homeomorphism $S^1\times S^1\to S^1\times S^1$.
For the trivial action of $G$ on a point, the shear map $G\to\mathrm{pt}\times\mathrm{pt}$ is surjective, but it is injective only if $G$ is trivial.

Non-example: for $S^1$ rotating $S^2$ about an axis, the shear map is neither injective, because the poles are fixed by every $g$, nor surjective, because points at different heights are never paired.

reminder: A Siegel zero is a hypothetical real zero of an [L-function](c:l-function) of a real [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character) that lies unusually close to $1$.
definition: Let $\chi$ be a real, non-principal [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character) modulo $q$. A Siegel zero is a real zero $\beta<1$ of the [L-function](c:l-function) $L(s,\chi)$ with $1-\beta$ much smaller than $1/\log q$. Siegel's theorem bounds $1-\beta$ from below by $c(\varepsilon)q^{-\varepsilon}$ with an ineffective constant, no Siegel zero is known, and the generalized Riemann hypothesis would exclude them.
examples: Hypothetical: a quadratic character $\chi_D$ whose $L(s,\chi_D)$ has a real zero $\beta$ with $1-\beta<0.01/\log|D|$; no such zero is known to exist.
Siegel's theorem says that any real zero satisfies $1-\beta\ge c(\varepsilon)|D|^{-\varepsilon}$, so it cannot be extremely close to $1$.
Under the generalized Riemann hypothesis, every zero in the critical strip has real part $1/2$, so there is no Siegel zero.
Non-example: the trivial zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ at non-positive integers are real but far from $1$, and the non-real zeros on the critical line are not real; neither kind is a Siegel zero.

reminder: A sieve on an object $X$ is a collection of morphisms into $X$ that is closed under precomposition.
definition: Let $X$ be an [object](c:object) of a [category](c:category) $\mathcal{C}$. A sieve on $X$ is a set $S$ of morphisms with codomain $X$ such that, if $f:Y\to X$ is in $S$ and $g:Z\to Y$ is any morphism, then the [composition](c:composition) $f\circ g$ is in $S$. Equivalently, a sieve on $X$ is a [subfunctor](c:subfunctor) of the representable [presheaf](c:presheaf) $\mathcal{C}(-,X)$.
examples: The set of all morphisms into $X$ is a sieve, the maximal sieve, and the empty set is a sieve, the empty sieve.
For a monoid viewed as a category with one object, a sieve is a right ideal.

On the poset of open sets of a space, a sieve on $U$ is a family of open subsets of $U$ closed under passing to smaller open sets; a cover $\{U_i\}$ of $U$ generates the sieve of all open sets inside some $U_i$.
Non-example: in the poset of open subsets of $(0,2)$, the family $\{(0,1)\}$ is not a sieve on $(0,2)$, since it does not contain the smaller open set $(0,\tfrac12)\subseteq(0,1)$.

steps: Let $I$ be a right [ideal in a monoid](c:ideal-in-a-monoid) $M$, and view $M$ as a category with one object $*$.
The elements of $I$ are morphisms with codomain $*$, and composition is multiplication in $M$.
Closure of $I$ under right multiplication by elements of $M$ is closure under precomposition.
So $I$ is a sieve on $*$.
links.why: It shows that a sieve is a right ideal where the monoid is replaced by a category with many objects.

steps: Take a Grothendieck topology $J$ on $\mathcal{C}$ and a [covering sieve](c:covering-sieve) $S\in J(X)$.
By definition, a covering sieve is a sieve on $X$ that belongs to $J(X)$.
So every covering sieve is a sieve.
The covering case adds membership in $J(X)$, which brings stability under pullback and a transitivity condition.
links.why: It shows that covering sieves are the sieves chosen by a topology, so sieves are the raw material of sheaf theory.

reminder: A sigma-complete Boolean algebra is a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) in which every countable family of elements has a supremum.
definition: A sigma-complete Boolean algebra is a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) $B$ in which every [countable](c:countable-set) subset has a least upper bound in $B$. By complementation, every countable subset then also has a greatest lower bound. Equivalently, $B$ is a Boolean algebra that is also a [sigma-complete lattice](c:sigma-complete-lattice).
examples: Every [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) of sets, such as the Borel sets of $\mathbb{R}$, is a sigma-complete Boolean algebra under union, intersection and complement.
The power set $\mathcal{P}(X)$ of a set $X$ is a sigma-complete Boolean algebra; it is even complete.
The measure algebra of the Borel sets modulo the null sets is a sigma-complete Boolean algebra.
Non-example: the algebra of finite and cofinite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is a Boolean algebra but is not sigma-complete, because the sets $\{2\},\{4\},\{6\},\dots$ have no least upper bound in it.

steps: Take a sigma-complete Boolean algebra $B$.
It is a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) by definition.
The sigma-complete case adds least upper bounds of all countable subsets.
links.why: It shows that a sigma-complete Boolean algebra is a Boolean algebra closed under countable joins and meets.

steps: Start with a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\Sigma$ of subsets of a set $X$, ordered by inclusion.
Union, intersection and complement make $\Sigma$ a Boolean algebra.
A countable union of members of $\Sigma$ lies in $\Sigma$, and it is their least upper bound.
So $\Sigma$ is a sigma-complete Boolean algebra.
links.why: It shows that sigma-algebras are the concrete case, and that sigma-complete Boolean algebras are their abstract form.

steps: Start with a [complete Boolean algebra](c:complete-boolean-algebra) $B$, where every subset has a supremum.
In particular, every countable subset has a supremum.
So $B$ is sigma-complete; the sigma-complete case asks only for countable subsets.
links.why: It shows that completeness is the strong form of sigma-completeness, with all subsets in place of countable ones.

reminder: A simplicial algebra is a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) in a category of algebras: algebras $A_n$ with face and degeneracy maps that are algebra homomorphisms.
definition: Fix a category of [algebras](c:algebra), such as commutative rings or associative algebras over a ring $k$. A simplicial algebra is a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) in it: a sequence of algebras $A_n$ for $n\ge0$, with algebra homomorphisms $d_i:A_n\to A_{n-1}$ and $s_i:A_n\to A_{n+1}$ that satisfy the simplicial identities. Equivalently, it is a functor $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Alg}$.
examples: A constant simplicial algebra has $A_n=A$ for all $n$, with all face and degeneracy maps equal to the identity.
A simplicial commutative ring is a simplicial algebra in commutative rings; its homotopy groups form a graded commutative ring.
A free simplicial resolution $P_\bullet\to R$ of a commutative ring $R$ by polynomial algebras computes derived tensor products.
Non-example: a simplicial vector space whose levels carry no compatible multiplication is not a simplicial algebra, because the multiplication must commute with every $d_i$ and $s_i$.

steps: Take a simplicial algebra $A_\bullet$.
It is a functor from $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ to a category of algebras, so it is a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object).
The algebra case adds that each $A_n$ is an algebra and every face and degeneracy map is an algebra homomorphism.
links.why: It shows that simplicial algebras are simplicial objects in a category of algebras, so simplicial tools apply to them.

reminder: A singular perturbation problem has a small parameter $\varepsilon$ such that its solutions do not converge uniformly to a solution of the problem at $\varepsilon=0$.
definition: A problem that depends on a small parameter $\varepsilon>0$ is a singular perturbation problem when setting $\varepsilon=0$ changes its nature: for example, it lowers the order of a [differential equation](c:differential-equation), or the solutions for $\varepsilon>0$ do not converge uniformly to a solution of the reduced problem. In a regular perturbation, by contrast, the solutions depend smoothly on $\varepsilon$ up to $\varepsilon=0$. Singular problems show boundary layers, fast and slow time scales, or roots that escape to infinity.
examples: For $\varepsilon y''+y'+y=0$ with $y(0)=0$ and $y(1)=1$, the reduced equation $y'+y=0$ has order $1$ and cannot meet both boundary conditions, so the solution has a boundary layer near $x=0$.
The fast-slow system $\varepsilon\dot x=f(x,y)$, $\dot y=g(x,y)$ is singular: at $\varepsilon=0$ it becomes the algebraic equation $f=0$, whose solution set is a [slow manifold](c:slow-manifold).
The equation $\varepsilon x^2+x-1=0$ has two roots for $\varepsilon\neq0$ but one root at $\varepsilon=0$; the second root, near $-1/\varepsilon$, escapes to infinity.
Non-example: $\dot y=-y+\varepsilon y^2$ with $y(0)=1$ is a regular perturbation, because the reduced problem has the same order and the solutions converge uniformly on bounded time intervals.

reminder: A special Jordan algebra is a [Jordan algebra](c:jordan-algebra) that embeds in an associative algebra with the product $a\circ b=\tfrac12(ab+ba)$.
definition: For an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over a field of characteristic not $2$, let $A^+$ be the same vector space with the Jordan product $a\circ b=\tfrac12(ab+ba)$. A [Jordan algebra](c:jordan-algebra) is special when it is isomorphic to a [subalgebra](c:subalgebra) of some $A^+$. A Jordan algebra that is not special is called exceptional.
examples: The real symmetric $n\times n$ matrices with $a\circ b=\tfrac12(ab+ba)$ form a special Jordan algebra, a subalgebra of $M_n(\mathbb{R})^+$.
The Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{C}$ or over the quaternions also form special Jordan algebras.
Every spin factor, the Jordan algebra of a quadratic form, is special, because it embeds in a Clifford algebra.
Non-example: the Albert algebra of $3\times3$ Hermitian octonionic matrices is not special (Albert, 1934); it is the standard exceptional Jordan algebra.

steps: Take a special Jordan algebra $J$ inside some $A^+$.
The product $a\circ b=\tfrac12(ab+ba)$ is commutative.
It satisfies the Jordan identity $(a\circ b)\circ a^2=a\circ(b\circ a^2)$, by associativity of $A$.
So $J$ is a [Jordan algebra](c:jordan-algebra); the special case adds an embedding into an associative algebra.
links.why: It shows that special Jordan algebras are the ones that come from associative algebras by symmetrizing the product.

reminder: The stabilization of an ∞-category $C$ with finite limits is the stable ∞-category of spectrum objects in $C$.
definition: Let $C$ be an [∞-category](c:infinity-1-category) with [finite limits](c:finite-limit). Its stabilization $\mathrm{Stab}(C)$ is the [stable ∞-category](c:stable-infinity-category) of [spectrum objects](c:spectrum-object) in the pointed objects $C_*$, which are sequences $(X_n)$ with equivalences $X_n\simeq\Omega X_{n+1}$ for the [loop space object](c:loop-space-object) functor $\Omega$. The functor $\Omega^\infty:\mathrm{Stab}(C)\to C$ is universal: for stable $D$, exact functors $D\to\mathrm{Stab}(C)$ correspond to left exact functors $D\to C$.
examples: For $C$ the ∞-category of spaces, $\mathrm{Stab}(C)$ is the ∞-category of spectra, and $\Omega^\infty$ takes a spectrum to its infinite loop space.
If $C$ is already stable, then $\mathrm{Stab}(C)\simeq C$.

Non-example: the suspension spectrum functor $\Sigma^\infty$ is not the stabilization; the stabilization is the category $\mathrm{Stab}(C)$, and $\Sigma^\infty$ is only a functor into it, left adjoint to $\Omega^\infty$ when $C$ is presentable.

reminder: A proper morphism factors as a morphism with connected fibers followed by a finite morphism.
definition: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a [proper morphism](c:is-proper) of Noetherian [schemes](c:scheme), and put $Y'=\mathbf{Spec}_Y f_*\mathcal{O}_X$. The Stein factorization of $f$ is $X\xrightarrow{g}Y'\xrightarrow{h}Y$, where $h$ is a [finite morphism](c:is-finite) and $g$ is proper with $g_*\mathcal{O}_X=\mathcal{O}_{Y'}$, so that the fibers of $g$ are [connected](c:connected-space).
examples: If $f$ is already finite, then $Y'=X$, so $g$ is the identity and $h=f$.
For the blow-up $f:X\to Y$ of a smooth variety along a smooth center, $f_*\mathcal{O}_X=\mathcal{O}_Y$, so $Y'=Y$ and $f$ has connected fibers.
For $X=Y\sqcup Y\to Y$, with the identity on each copy, one gets $Y'=Y\sqcup Y$; then $g$ is an isomorphism and $h$ is the fold map, of degree $2$.
Non-example: the open immersion $\mathbb{A}^1\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{A}^1$ is not proper, and $f_*\mathcal{O}$ is not a finite $\mathcal{O}_Y$-module, so it has no Stein factorization in this sense.

reminder: Stone duality is a contravariant equivalence between Boolean algebras and Stone spaces, using ultrafilters in one direction and clopen sets in the other.
definition: Stone duality is the contravariant equivalence between the category of [Boolean algebras](c:boolean-algebra) and the category of [Stone spaces](c:stone-space), which are compact Hausdorff spaces with a base of [clopen](c:clopen-subset) sets. It sends a Boolean algebra $B$ to the space of its [ultrafilters](c:ultrafilter), with basic open sets $\{U:b\in U\}$ for $b\in B$. It sends a Stone space $X$ to the Boolean algebra of its clopen subsets, and the two constructions are inverse up to isomorphism.
examples: A finite Boolean algebra $\mathcal{P}(X)$ corresponds to the finite discrete space $X$ of its atoms.
The Boolean algebra of clopen subsets of the Cantor set is the countable atomless Boolean algebra.
The Boolean algebra $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ corresponds to the Stone-Čech compactification $\beta\mathbb{N}$, the space of ultrafilters on $\mathbb{N}$.
Non-example: the interval $[0,1]$ is compact Hausdorff but not a Stone space; its only clopen sets are $\emptyset$ and $[0,1]$, so its clopen algebra forgets the space.

reminder: A stratified space is a topological space split into locally closed strata whose closures are unions of strata.
definition: A stratified space is a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ with a decomposition into disjoint locally closed subspaces $S_\alpha$, the strata. It satisfies the frontier condition: the closure of each stratum is a union of strata. Often each stratum is a [manifold](c:manifold), and the decomposition comes from a [stratification](c:stratification) $\emptyset=X_{-1}\subset X_0\subset\cdots\subset X_n=X$ by closed subsets, with strata $X_i\setminus X_{i-1}$.
examples: A simplicial complex is stratified by its open simplices.
A manifold with boundary is stratified by its interior and its boundary.
The cone $\{x^2+y^2=z^2\}\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ is stratified by its vertex and the rest of the cone.
Non-example: the decomposition of $\mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ is not a stratification, because neither piece is locally closed.

steps: Take a stratified space $X$ with strata $S_\alpha$.
Forget the decomposition into strata.
What remains is the [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$.
The stratified case adds a decomposition into locally closed strata that satisfies the frontier condition.
links.why: It shows that a stratified space is a topological space with extra data, so all topological results still apply.

steps: Take a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ and use the single stratum $S=M$.
The stratum $M$ is locally closed in $M$.
Its closure is the union of strata, namely $M$, so the frontier condition holds.
So $M$ is a stratified space with one stratum.
links.why: It shows that stratified spaces allow singular points that manifolds exclude.

reminder: A dynamical system is structurally stable when every small perturbation of it has the same orbit structure, up to a homeomorphism.
definition: Let $X$ be a $C^1$ [vector field](c:vector-field) on a compact [manifold](c:compact-manifold) $M$. It is structurally stable when there is a $C^1$-neighborhood $\mathcal{U}$ of $X$ such that for every $Y\in\mathcal{U}$ some [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) of $M$ maps each oriented orbit of $X$ onto an oriented orbit of $Y$. The same definition applies to a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, with a topological conjugacy in place of the orbit map.
examples: On the circle, the flow of $\dot\theta=\sin\theta$ is structurally stable: a small perturbation still has exactly one source and one sink.

Every [Morse-Smale system](c:morse-smale-system) is structurally stable (Palis-Smale), and by Peixoto's theorem the structurally stable vector fields on a compact orientable surface are exactly the Morse-Smale ones.
An Anosov diffeomorphism, such as the cat map $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ on the torus, is structurally stable (Anosov).

Non-example: a vector field with a center, such as $\dot x=y$, $\dot y=-x$ near the origin, is not structurally stable, because the perturbation $\dot x=y+\varepsilon x$, $\dot y=-x+\varepsilon y$ turns the closed orbits into spirals.

reminder: A symmetric sequence is a sequence of objects $X(n)$ in which each $X(n)$ carries an action of the symmetric group $\Sigma_n$.
definition: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a [category](c:category), usually symmetric monoidal with coproducts. A symmetric sequence in $\mathcal{C}$ is a [sequence](c:sequence) of objects $X(0),X(1),X(2),\dots$ together with an [action](c:group-action) of the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $\Sigma_n$ on each $X(n)$. Equivalently, it is a functor from the groupoid of finite sets and bijections to $\mathcal{C}$.
examples: In vector spaces over $k$, the sequence $X(n)=k[\Sigma_n]$ of regular representations is a symmetric sequence.
The underlying symmetric sequence of an [operad](c:operad) $P$ is $(P(n))_{n\ge0}$ with the $\Sigma_n$-actions of the operad; for the commutative operad, $P(n)=k$ with trivial actions.
A symmetric sequence of sets is a [species](c:species); for example, the species of linear orders has $L(n)=\Sigma_n$, acted on by relabeling.
Non-example: a plain sequence of vector spaces $(V_n)$ with no action of $\Sigma_n$ is not a symmetric sequence, because the actions are part of the data.

steps: Start with a [species](c:species), a functor $F$ from finite sets and bijections to sets.
Each set $F(\{1,\dots,n\})$ carries an action of $\Sigma_n$ by relabeling.
So $(F(\{1,\dots,n\}))_n$ is a sequence of sets with $\Sigma_n$-actions, a symmetric sequence in sets.
A general symmetric sequence allows values in any category $\mathcal{C}$, not only in sets.
links.why: It shows that symmetric sequences are species with values in an arbitrary category.

steps: Start with a symmetric sequence $X$ in $\mathcal{C}$.
Choose a set of colors with exactly one element.
With one color, a [colored symmetric sequence](c:colored-symmetric-sequence) is a sequence of objects $X(n)$ with $\Sigma_n$-actions.
So $X$ is a colored symmetric sequence with one color.
links.why: It shows that colored symmetric sequences extend symmetric sequences to several colors, as for operads with many colors.
